accordion.title: How is this calculated?
accordion.emi_plain: An Equated Monthly Installment (EMI) is a fixed monthly payment where every installment covers both accrued monthly interest and part of the principal. In the early months, interest makes up most of the installment; over time, the principal portion steadily increases until the loan is fully paid off.
accordion.emi_where: Where E = Monthly EMI, P = Principal loan amount, r = Monthly interest rate (Annual Rate / 12 / 100), n = Loan tenure in months.
accordion.goal_plain: Because Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) installments are deposited at the start of each month (annuity-due), every rupee immediately compounds. When inflation adjustment is enabled, your target corpus is compounded forward at the inflation rate to preserve its future purchasing power.
accordion.goal_formula:
Monthly SIP = FV_adjusted / [ (((1 + r)^n - 1) / r) × (1 + r) ]
FV_adjusted = Target × (1 + inflation)^years
accordion.goal_where: Where Target = Target corpus in today's money, r = Monthly return rate, n = Total months, inflation = Annual inflation rate.
accordion.compound_plain: Compounding means your investment earnings earn their own earnings over time. For monthly SIPs, money compounds on every new deposit. For lump-sum deposits, interest compounds based on the chosen compounding frequency. Starting even a few years earlier delivers a dramatic exponential multiplier.
accordion.compound_formula:
SIP FV = P × [ ((1 + r)^n - 1) / r ] × (1 + r)
Lump Sum A = P × (1 + r / m)^(m × t)
accordion.compound_where: Where P = Monthly deposit or Initial principal, r = Annual return rate, m = Compounding frequency per year, t = Years, n = Total months (t × 12).

lesson1.title: Needs vs Wants: The Envelope Filter
lesson1.summary: Needs keep you alive and functioning; wants make life enjoyable. Conflating the two is the #1 reason budgets fail.
lesson1.content: A need is non-negotiable: basic monthly grocery ration, rent, utility bills, medication, or study tuition. A want is an upgrade: eating out, brand upgrades, OTT subscriptions, or impulsive shopping. In Household mode, grocery ration is a need, but ordering fancy restaurant takeout is a want. In Student mode, hostel mess and exam books are needs; daily cafe hangouts and gaming passes are wants. The golden rule is simple: fund needs first, cap wants at 30% of your discretionary allowance, and never take an EMI or debt for a want.
lesson1.takeaway: Buy what you need, budget what you want, and never take an EMI for luxury.
lesson1.quiz_q: Which of the following is considered a 'Want' rather than a 'Need'?
lesson1.quiz_opt_1: Basic monthly grocery ration for the household
lesson1.quiz_opt_2: Upgrading to the newest smartphone when your current phone works fine
lesson1.quiz_opt_3: Monthly electricity and cooking gas bill
lesson1.quiz_expl: Upgrading a perfectly working phone is a lifestyle upgrade (want). Core groceries and home utilities are survival needs.

lesson2.title: 50/30/20: Why We Adapt It for India
lesson2.summary: The textbook 50/30/20 rule breaks down in Indian cities where rent and EMIs often take 60% of income. Here is our adaptive formula.
lesson2.content: Western finance says 50% Needs, 30% Wants, 20% Savings. But in India, high urban rents, family support, or college fees mean fixed commitments often exceed 50%. If you strictly follow the textbook rule, you feel guilty and abandon budgeting altogether. PennyPath adapts it: 1) Lock your Fixed Commitments first (Rent + EMIs + Bills). 2) Secure a Savings Target (aim for 20%, but start with whatever is feasible, even 10%). 3) Whatever remains is your Discretionary Allowance (D), converted into a Daily Safe-to-Spend limit (D / 30). No guilt, pure math.
lesson2.takeaway: Fixed expenses first, pay yourself savings second, divide the rest by 30 for daily peace of mind.
lesson2.quiz_q: In PennyPath's adapted formula, what is calculated after securing fixed expenses and savings?
lesson2.quiz_opt_2: Taking a personal loan to cover the gap
lesson2.quiz_expl: Daily safe-to-spend (D / 30) gives you an exact daily benchmark so you never accidentally overspend into savings.

lesson3.title: Emergency Fund: Your Financial Airbag
lesson3.summary: An emergency fund is money kept purely for unexpected shocks — job loss, medical urgency, or urgent home repairs.
lesson3.content: Without an emergency buffer, a single medical bill or broken appliance forces you into high-interest debt or credit card loans. In Household mode, target 3 to 6 months of mandatory living expenses (rent, ration, EMIs, utilities) in a high-yield liquid FD or sweep-in account. In Student mode, maintain a 1-to-2 month buffer for exam fees, laptop repairs, or emergency travel home. This money is NOT for Diwali sales, holiday trips, or stock market trading. It exists for peaceful sleep at night.
lesson3.takeaway: Build a 3-6 month safety buffer before you start investing in equities.
lesson3.quiz_q: Where should an emergency fund ideally be parked?
lesson3.quiz_opt_1: Volatile crypto tokens or intraday stock trades
lesson3.quiz_opt_2: High-safety liquid bank FD or sweep-in savings account
lesson3.quiz_opt_3: Locked in a real estate land plot
lesson3.quiz_expl: Emergency funds must be 100% liquid and principal-safe, accessible within hours during an emergency.

lesson4.title: How EMIs Really Work: Reducing Balance Truth
lesson4.summary: Monthly installments look small, but interest is front-loaded in the early months. And 'No-Cost EMI' is rarely free.
lesson4.content: When you take a loan, banks use the 'reducing balance' method. In the first year of a 3-year bike or personal loan, up to 60-70% of each EMI goes toward paying interest, not reducing your principal. Furthermore, retailer 'No-Cost EMI' offers typically hide costs in two ways: 1) You forfeit an upfront 5-10% cash discount, and 2) The bank charges a non-refundable processing fee (₹199-₹499) PLUS 18% GST on the interest subvention. If you must borrow, check the total payable amount, not just the monthly figure.
lesson4.takeaway: Calculate total cost including GST and fees before choosing an EMI over cash.
lesson4.quiz_q: Why is a 'No-Cost EMI' often more expensive than paying upfront in cash?
lesson4.quiz_opt_1: Banks add processing fees and 18% GST on interest discount, and you forfeit upfront cash discounts
lesson4.quiz_opt_2: The merchant delivers the product slower
lesson4.quiz_opt_3: It is completely prohibited by law
lesson4.quiz_expl: Banks charge 18% GST on the interest discount and processing charges, making 'free' EMIs cost extra money.

lesson5.title: Compound Interest: The Power of Starting Early
lesson5.summary: Time in the market matters far more than the amount you invest. Starting with ₹1,000 at age 20 beats ₹5,000 at age 35.
lesson5.content: Simple interest pays return only on your initial deposit. Compound interest pays return on your principal PLUS all previously accumulated returns. In the first 5 years, the growth feels painfully slow. But after 10-15 years, the curve turns vertical — your money earns more than your salary. A 20-year-old student putting away just ₹1,000 every month at 12% annual return builds over ₹35 Lakhs by age 50 with only ₹3.6 Lakhs total investment. Delaying by just 10 years cuts that future wealth by more than half.
lesson5.takeaway: Start small today. Time is the engine of compound growth, not timing the market.
lesson5.quiz_q: What makes compound interest grow exponentially over long periods?
lesson5.quiz_opt_1: Interest is earned on accumulated interest, not just principal
lesson5.quiz_opt_2: The government doubles the money every five years
lesson5.quiz_expl: By reinvesting returns, your earning base expands exponentially each year like a snowball rolling downhill.

lesson6.title: SIP vs Lump Sum: Why Regular Habits Win
lesson6.summary: Trying to time market peaks and valleys causes panic. SIP turns market volatility into your biggest advantage.
lesson6.content: A Lump Sum puts all your money into the market on a single day. If the market crashes the next week, you suffer immediate loss and panic. A Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) invests a fixed sum (e.g., ₹1,000 or ₹5,000) on the same date every month regardless of market mood. When the market is high, your money buys fewer mutual fund units; when the market drops, your money buys MORE units at discount prices. This is called 'Rupee Cost Averaging'. For salaried earners and students, SIP removes emotional stress and builds automatic discipline.
lesson6.takeaway: Don't time the market. Automate a monthly SIP on salary day and let averaging work for you.
lesson6.quiz_q: How does a monthly SIP benefit an investor during a stock market downturn?
lesson6.quiz_opt_1: It automatically buys more units at lower prices (Rupee Cost Averaging)
lesson6.quiz_opt_2: The bank refunds all your temporary market losses
lesson6.quiz_opt_3: The SIP automatically stops trading during drops
lesson6.quiz_expl: Lower NAV during downturns allows your fixed monthly SIP amount to accumulate more mutual fund units.

lesson7.title: Inflation: The Silent Thief of Bank Deposits
lesson7.summary: Leaving cash in a 3% savings bank account feels safe, but at 6% inflation, your money loses purchasing power every year.
lesson7.content: Inflation is the steady rise in prices over time. In India, consumer inflation historically averages around 5% to 7% per year. What cost ₹100 a decade ago costs over ₹180 today (from milk and school books to hospital visits). If your money sits in a regular bank savings account earning 3% interest, you are losing approximately 3% in real purchasing power every single year. Keeping money in cash or low-interest accounts is safe from nominal loss, but guaranteed to suffer real purchasing power destruction. Beat inflation by keeping only emergency funds in liquid FDs and putting long-term savings in growth assets.
lesson7.takeaway: Idle money loses purchasing power. Invest long-term savings where returns beat the 6% inflation benchmark.
lesson7.quiz_q: If bank savings interest is 3% and inflation is 6%, what happens to your money's real value?
lesson7.quiz_opt_1: Purchasing power decreases by roughly 3% each year
lesson7.quiz_opt_2: Purchasing power doubles in five years
lesson7.quiz_opt_3: There is no change in purchasing power
lesson7.quiz_expl: Real return = nominal rate (3%) - inflation (6%) = -3%. Your cash buys fewer goods over time.

lesson8.title: Risk vs Return: The Twin Sides of Investing
lesson8.summary: Higher return requires enduring short-term volatility. Safe assets protect capital but fail against inflation.
lesson8.content: Risk in finance doesn't mean gambling; it means the degree of fluctuation (volatility) your investment experiences along the way. Assets with guaranteed principal — like Bank Fixed Deposits (FD) or Government Savings Schemes — have near-zero volatility, but their returns (~6.5-7%) barely beat inflation and taxes. Equities and Index Funds, on the other hand, can drop 15% in a bad year, but historically deliver 11-13% annual compound growth over 7+ years. Match your risk to your time horizon: money needed in under 2 years belongs in FDs; money needed after 5+ years belongs in equities.
lesson8.takeaway: Never put short-term money in equities, and never leave long-term wealth solely in fixed deposits.
lesson8.quiz_q: For a financial goal you must pay within 12 months, where should the money be parked?
lesson8.quiz_opt_1: Safe Fixed Deposit or Liquid Fund with zero equity exposure
lesson8.quiz_opt_2: High-risk small-cap stocks for fast multiplication
lesson8.quiz_expl: Short-term horizons cannot afford equity market corrections; capital preservation and liquidity are paramount.

lesson9.title: The Bharat Trio: Gold, FD, and Mutual Funds
lesson9.summary: Understand the three pillars of Indian household wealth and how to balance them for safety and growth.
lesson9.content: Indian personal finance thrives on a three-pillar balance: 1) Fixed Deposits (FD): Unmatched peace of mind and liquidity for emergencies or short-term bills. 2) Gold (Sovereign Gold Bonds or Digital Gold): Cultural pride and a proven hedge during global geopolitical crises and rupee depreciation (prefer gold ETFs or digital gold over jewelry with 20% making charges). 3) Mutual Funds (Nifty 50 Index Funds): The wealth generator that lets ordinary citizens profit from India's corporate economic growth. A balanced household might hold 25% FD for safety, 15% Gold for crisis protection, and 60% Index Funds for future goals.
lesson9.takeaway: FD gives stability, Gold gives crisis protection, Mutual Funds build long-term wealth. Hold all three in proper balance.
lesson9.quiz_q: Which investment vehicle provides the most cost-effective way to invest in gold without losing money on making charges?
lesson9.quiz_opt_1: Gold ETFs or Sovereign Digital Gold without making charges
lesson9.quiz_opt_2: Buying physical jewelry with 20% craftsmanship fees
lesson9.quiz_expl: Gold ETFs track pure 24K gold prices with zero making charges or storage risks.

lesson10.title: Spotting Scams: The 'Guaranteed Return' Trap
lesson10.summary: If an investment scheme promises high, guaranteed returns with zero risk, it is 100% a fraud. Protect your money.
lesson10.content: Financial fraudsters prey on two human emotions: greed and urgency. Common Indian traps include: 1) 'Double your money in 3 months' Ponzi schemes; 2) VIP Telegram/WhatsApp stock tip channels charging subscription fees; 3) Unregistered app-based loan traps that access your contacts; 4) 'Part-time work' scams paying small amounts for YouTube likes before demanding deposits. The cardinal rule of finance: High returns are mathematically impossible without high risk. Legitimate brokers and mutual funds are strictly registered with SEBI or RBI. Always verify registration on sebi.gov.in before transferring a single rupee.
lesson10.takeaway: Guaranteed high return + zero risk = 100% scam. Always verify SEBI/RBI registration.
lesson10.quiz_q: What is the biggest red flag that an investment offer is a fraudulent scam?
lesson10.quiz_opt_1: Promising high 'guaranteed' returns with zero risk or volatility
lesson10.quiz_opt_2: Being registered with SEBI and listed on the NSE stock exchange
lesson10.quiz_opt_3: Providing audited regulatory annual financial statements
lesson10.quiz_expl: Genuine market investments always carry market risk. Anyone guaranteeing high risk-free return is running a scam.

about.problem: Pennypath exists to help Indians take control of their personal finances through intelligent envelope budgeting. Many people struggle to track spending, save consistently, and plan for future goals without feeling overwhelmed by complex financial tools.
about.problemDescription: Our mission is to provide a simple, offline-first financial management platform that adapts to Indian lifestyles - whether you are a student managing pocket money, a household managing family expenses, or a first-job earner navigating EMIs and savings.
about.visionDescription: To become India's most trusted personal finance companion, enabling every Indian to budget smartly, save consistently, and grow wealth responsibly - all while keeping their data private and their finances completely offline.
